The performance of the proposed COLREGs compliant RL algorithm is assessed under the path-following environment shown in Fig. 1. A standard laptop with Intel i7-4700HQ CPU, Nvidia GTX 765M GPU is used to train and test the proposed approach. We compare the per formance of the four proposed agents (Q-learning, Double Q-learning, Deep Q-learning, and Double Deep Q-learning) under the hyperparam eters of Tables 3 and 4. For more robust results, the training process is entirely iterated 10 times to provide the average, minimum and maximum of each features under study.

Proximity-responsive hazard avoidance is where a USV, following a set course, needs to adjust its response in time to effectively avoid a collision with an obstacle if the un certainty of a dynamic obstacle is detected suddenly. In contrast, close-range collision avoidance requires consideration of the vessel’s shape and turning angle. Hazard avoid ance and multi-vessel collision avoidance in complex marine conditions are also hot topics of current research.

5. Cluster Path Planning
USVs cluster path planning technology is rapidly developing as a core key technol ogy. USVs cluster path planning is the key to cluster path generation, obstacle avoidance, collision avoidance, and other navigation and coordination tasks assignment. It is essen tially a multi-constrained combinatorial optimization algorithm. The cluster intelligence optimization algorithm focusing on the bionic approach and the multi-task assignment strategy are essential assets to solve the cluster path planning problem [111].

To achieve the autonomous navigation of USV in the practical ocean environment, three critical problems need to be addressed. Firstly, it should be fast and efficient in processing environmental data and searching paths. Secondly, the generated path should maintain a safe distance between the USV and the coastline. Thirdly, it should generate a feasible and optimal energy-efficient path in a complex ocean envi­ ronment including the time-variant sea current.

3.3. ALSEE path planning method
The ALSEE path generation includes three steps. First, the mission goal point is inserted into the expanded coastline map, and ALS is applied to obtain the relative USV velocity matrix. Second, we combined the sea current data and applied an energy consumption model to calculate the weight of each node in the configuration space. Third, a gradient descent method was implemented to search for an energy efficient path from the origin to the goal point.

In the event of sea current changes, the energy weight map of the USV is updated using the current sea current data. The gradient descent method is again applied to research the path based on the current po­ sition of the USV. This process enables the completion of energy-efficient path replanning in a time-varying sea current environment.

4.1. Energy efficiency comparison
To demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed ALSEE method, the performance of the ALSEE, ALS, Voronoi energy efficiency (VEE) (Niu et al., 2018), Voronoi-visibility energy-efficient (VVEE) (Niu et al., 2018), and improved Voronoi-A* energy-efficient (IVAEE) (Zhang et al., 2022) methods were studied in terms of energy efficiency and naviga­ tion time efficiency. The ALS method was used to search for the shortest paths, and the other methods were used to search for energy-efficient paths. To visualise the performance of each method, we demonstrated its performance using a single USV mission.

D. Rationale for Choosing BLS for Critic Networks Rather Than Actor Networks
The BLS is uniquely suitable for critic networks due to its strength in regression tasks through ridge regression. It aligns with the role of the critic network in actor-critic algorithms, which is the estimation of Q values. In contrast, the actor network learns a policy function (i.e., a probability distribution or deterministic action), which requires gradient-based optimization to maximize expected returns.

Thus, the hybrid architecture (i.e., BLS critic with DNN actor) balances the computational eﬃciency (via BLS regression) and gradient-based policy optimization (via DNNs). Future work may explore BLS-based actors for stochastic policies without compromising eﬃciency, but it remains an open problem.

III. FORMATION TRACKING CONTROLLER DESIGN
First, we design a collision avoidance resilient distributed formation estimator. Then, the formation tracking error can converge to a residual set of predeﬁned accuracy within a preassigned settling time by using estimated state signals and designing a transformation function. Meanwhile, intermittent actuator faults are effectively compensated through the employ ment of adaptive techniques. text: To reinforce maritime sovereignty preservation and effectively control potential security threats targets, a gated communication attention-based multi-agent deep deterministic policy gradient (GCA-MADDPG) algorithm for multiple unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) collaborative hunting decision-making strategy is proposed in this study. The innovations of proposed method are: (1) the combination of intention sharing and attention communication effectively mitigates the communication overhead among the USV cluster, empowering each member to autonomously determine their optimal communication targets; (2) the reward function design in­ corporates the Apollonius circle, speed, distance, and other re

3.5 More HAML Instances
In this subsection, we exemplify how HAML can be used for derivation of principled MARL algorithms, solely by constructing valid drift functional, neighborhood operator, and sam pling distribution. Our goal is to verify the correctness of HAML theory and enrich the cooperative MARL with more theoretically guaranteed and practical algorithms. The re sults are more robust heterogeneous-agent versions of popular RL algorithms including A2C, DDPG, and TD3, diﬀerent from those in Section 2.3.2.

3.5.3 HATD3
HATD3 improves HADDPG with tricks proposed by Fujimoto et al. (2018).
Similar to HADDPG, HATD3 is also an oﬀ-policy algorithm and optimises the same target, but it employs target policy smoothing, clipped double Q-learning, and delayed policy updates techniques (see Appendix G for full pseudocode). We observe that HATD3 consistently outperforms HADDPG on all tasks, showing that relevant reinforcement learning can be directly applied to MARL without the need for rediscovery, another beneﬁt of the HAML.

B. Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL)
A joint space representation does not scale well with large number of robots and makes it challenging to train and deploy deep neural network policies. Foerster et al. [24] provided an RL framework to explicitly learn communication protocols.

The theoretical properties of GNNs on transferability, scal ability and stability render them more suitable for decentral ized systems than MARL framework. Furthermore, imitation learning often helps in converging to a good policy faster than exploring a large action space in the reinforcement learning framework. An interesting approach would be to use imitation learning for an initial policy and then fine-tune using RL frameworks to improve performance.

id: LPAC Learnable Perception-Action-Communication-TRO2025-2401.04855v4:p6:c047
text:
A. Perception Module
The perception module is composed of a convolutional neural network (CNN) that takes a four-channel image as input and generates a 32-dimensional feature vector. The channels are grids of pre-defined size (32×32) and are centered around the current position of the robot. The first and the second chan nels are local representations of the importance and boundary maps, respectively. The other two channels, neighbor maps, encode the relative positions of the neighboring robots. Fig. 3 shows an example of the four-channel image, which forms the input to the CNN.

id: LPAC Learnable Perception-Action-Communication-TRO2025-2401.04855v4:p6:c051
text: ordinate. We normalize the relative coordinates by the communication range. If two or more neighboring robots are present in the same region of a pixel, the pixel is assigned the sum of the normalized relative coordinates of the neighboring robots. The neighbor maps are designed in this way to ensure that they are permutation invariant, i.e., the relative positions of the neighboring robots are independent of the order in which they are encoded in the map.

id: LPAC Learnable Perception-Action-Communication-TRO2025-2401.04855v4:p6:c052
text: These four channels are concatenated to form the input to the CNN. The CNN is composed of three sequences of a convolutional layer followed by batch normalization [49] and a leaky ReLU pointwise nonlinearity. The convolution layers have a kernel size of 3 × 3 and a stride of one with zero padding and generate 32 output channels. The output of the last sequence is flattened and passed through a linear layer with a leaky ReLU activation to generate a 32-dimensional feature vector. The feature vector is then sent to the communication module for further processing.

A. MLP Positional Encoding (MLP-PE)
A simple way to include positional information is to learn an MLP that maps positions, pi, to a same-dimensional vector as the input, xi. The MLP-PE is added to the input embedding:
zi = xi + MLP(pi) (32)
where MLP: R2 7→Rd is a multi-layer perceptron (MLP).
The embeddings zi become inputs to self-attention instead of xi. For models comprising multiple self-attention layers with residual connections, the MLP-PE is added only to the first layer. Residual connections propagate the positional information through to subsequent layers.

I. INTRODUCTION
A. Research Background D
UE to the rapid advancements in intelligent and uncrewed ships, along with the increasing demand for marine resource development, uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) have gained widespread usage in marine sampling, envi ronmental monitoring, hydro-logical measurement, maritime search and rescue, and port surveillance [1], [2], [3]. As such, they have emerged as a crucial area of focus in future ship research and development, with signiﬁcant implications for the maritime shipping industry.

By appropriately adjusting speed and heading, navigation efﬁciency can be enhanced while minimizing EC to the maximum extent possible. Therefore, it holds signiﬁcant research signiﬁcance and practical value to incorporate speed into the realm of path planning considera tions and achieving coordinated speed and heading planning.

A key question is whether our proposed method can adapt to ships of varying sizes and dynamic properties. (1) The agent observes the current state (St).
(2) The agent uses St to perform a suitable action (At) and provides it to the environment.
(3) The environment communicates the next state (St+1) and reward for the action to the agent.
(4) The agent performs the next action according to the reward received from the envi ronment.
(5) By repeating the above processes, the agent continuously implements actions to obtain the maximum reward.

Action masking then restricts the RL agent to this set of veriﬁed rule-compliant actions. In numerical evaluations on critical maritime trafﬁc situations, our agent always complies with the formalized legal rules and never collides while achieving a high goal-reaching rate during training and deployment. A. Safety Value Function
Safety is of the utmost importance. When external distur bances exist, we must ensure safety under worst-case scenarios.
A fundamental fact from safe control research is that only those states inside a subset of the constraint set, called robust invariant set, can achieve persistent safety [21]. For states outside the robust invariant set, there always exist some adversarial distur bances that will drive the system to violate the safety constraints regardless of what control policy is adopted. Therefore, enforc ing safety is essentially equivalent to constraining the system states inside the robust invariant set.

State transitions are determined by environmental dynamics, encompassing the USV model, target motion pattern, obstacle dynamics, and sensor noise. 4.1 Experimental Settings
In this section, we present the simulation results and performance analysis of the proposed CTRIP algorithm in terms of tracking success rate and collisions. The design of this environment is elaborated in detail from three core perspectives: environmental complexity, control constraints, and vessel attributes.
The experiments are conducted in a computer with an Inter (R) core (TM) i7-12700KF CPU, 32G of RAM and a NVIDIA GeForce RTX4070 graphics card. The operating system is Windows 11, and the GPU driver and CUDA versions are 565.90 and 11.7, respectively.
The simulated environment is developed based on OpenAI’s Particle Environment (a flexible frame

id: SCIS:p11:c051
text:
4.1.1 Environmental Complexity
To simulate real-world scenarios, the environment incorporates multiple dynamic and random factors:
• Ocean current influence: The global environmental conditions include the impact of ocean currents; • Perceptual interference: Random perceptual noise is introduced to mimic real-world sensing uncer tainties;
• Dynamic obstacles: After satisfying specific spatial constraints, each obstacle is assigned attributes, a random position, a random size, and a random speed.

id: SCIS:p11:c052
text:
4.1.2 Control Constraints
The control logic for the agent and the target is designed with distinct rules to reflect task characteristics:
Agent Vessel Control.
The agent vessel operates with a fixed speed of 3 m/s, so its action space is reduced to a one-dimensional set {ψt}, where ψt denotes the steering angle at time step t.
Target Vessel Control.
Three target modes are supported to adapt to different tracking scenarios:
• Static mode: The target is initialized at a position far from the agent to ensure sufficient tracking distance;
• Linear mode: The target moves in a uniform straight line along its initial direction; • Random mode: The target will move at a constant speed with slight ran

id: SCIS:p11:c053

III. OUR APPROACH
A. Overview & Assumptions
Our goal is to learn a robot navigation policy capable of local obstacle avoidance among unknown static and dynamic obstacles via reinforcement learning, while relying only on a global path and 2D lidar readings as input, compare Fig. 2a).
The global path is planned using A* in a map containing the known static obstacles of the environment. The dynamics of the moving obstacles are unknown to the robot and are implicitly learned from subsequent lidar readings for collision-free navigation.

目前, 多项研究已经初步验证了深度强化学习在多机器人编队避障控制中的有效性. Bai 等[16] 设计了一种 多机器人自适应编队控制框架, 能够使得机器人独立调整编队以通过障碍区域. Sadhukhan 等[17] 提出了一种基 于近端策略优化(proximal policy optimization, PPO) 的编队控制方法, 用于控制二阶完整约束智能体在障碍场 中进行导航. Xie 等[18] 通过深度Q 网络(deep Q-network, DQN) 设计智能体的编队控制策略模块, 实现了易于 训练且有效的编队避障控制. 然而, 上述方法均未充分考虑安全性问题. 由于环境具有不确定性和复杂性, 因此 智能体在策略学习的过程中需要对未知领域进行探索, 可能会采取不安全或不合理的动作, 从而导致学习到不 安全策略等问题.
因此, 设计具有安全性保证的强化学习方法正日益受到人们的关注与重视. 2015 年, Garcia 等[19] 提出了安 全强化学习(safe reinforcement learning, SRL) 的概念, 即确保学习系统合理性表现或遵守安全约束的强化学习 方法. 安全强化学习明确地将安全性约束纳入学习算法中, 确保智能体在学习过程中始终满足这些约束
